---
title: "Getting started"
---

## Imports

The examples on this site import the frame class and phibble's functions like
this:

```php
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phibble\{tibble, tribble};
use function Phibble\Expr\{col, desc, mean, n};
```

`Phibble\Expr` has functions named `min`, `max`, `sum`, `round`, `abs`, `log`,
`floor`, `str_pad`, `str_split`, `str_replace`, and a few others that share
names with PHP built-ins. In a file that imports
them, a bare `round($x)` calls phibble's expression helper. Write `\round($x)`
for PHP's function.

## Building frames

`tibble()` builds a frame column by column. Each named argument is a column.
A list gives one value per row, and a single value is repeated for every row.
A closure receives the frame built so far, so a column can be computed from
earlier ones.

{{< include examples/_tibble.md >}}

`tribble()` takes the column names first and then one list per row, which is
easier to read for small literal tables:

{{< include examples/_tribble.md >}}

`DataFrame::fromRows()` takes a list of associative arrays. Keys missing from a row
are NA. `DataFrame::fromColumns()` takes an array of columns and accepts explicit
types.

{{< include examples/_from-rows.md >}}

`DataFrame::fromCsv()` reads a CSV file and guesses each column's type. The
[input and output guide](io.qmd) covers its options.

## Printing

`echo $df` prints the frame the way tibble does. The header gives the size,
each column shows its type, and frames with more than 20 rows show the first
10. Numbers show three significant digits and NA prints as `NA` (or `<NA>` in
text columns).

{{< include examples/_read-csv.md >}}

`glimpse()` returns one line per column, which suits wide frames:

{{< include examples/_glimpse.md >}}

`format(n: 30, width: 120)` prints more rows or a wider table.

## Types and NA

Each column has one type from the `Phibble\Type` enum: `Float`, `Int`, `Bool`,
`String`, `Factor`, `Date`, `DateTime`, or `List`. Types are inferred from the
values, and PHP `null` is NA in every type. The [types guide](types.qmd)
describes inference, casts, and factors.

## Reading values

A column reads as a PHP list with `$df->name`, `$df['name']`, or
`$df->column('name')`. Rows are `Phibble\Row` objects, which read values as
properties or array keys. Iterating a frame yields its rows. An unknown column
name throws `Phibble\Exception\ColumnNotFound`; names are never matched
partially.

{{< include examples/_access.md >}}

## Verbs

DataFrames have the dplyr verbs as methods: `select()`, `filter()`, `mutate()`,
`rename()`, `arrange()`, `groupBy()`, `summarise()`, `distinct()`, `slice()`,
`head()`, and `join()`. Each returns a new frame.

`filter()` and `mutate()` accept a row closure, which receives a `Row` and
returns a value. `arrange()` takes column names, or `[name, 'desc']` pairs.

{{< include examples/_verbs.md >}}

The same verbs accept [expressions](expr.qmd) built with `col()` and the helper
functions. Expressions are evaluated a whole column at a time, and they are the
form that SQL and Polars backends can translate.

{{< include examples/_verbs-expr.md >}}

## Groups

`groupBy()` records grouping columns on the frame. `summarise()` returns one
row per group, with groups in sorted order and NA last, as dplyr does. With
several grouping columns, the result keeps all but the last.

{{< include examples/_tour.md >}}

In a grouped frame, `filter()` and `mutate()` work within each group. An
aggregate inside `mutate()` is computed per group and repeated for each of the
group's rows:

{{< include examples/_grouped.md >}}

A row closure receives the row's group as its second argument:
`fn (Row $r, DataFrame $group) => ...`.

By default, groups are the combinations that occur in the data. With
`groupBy($names, drop: false)`, as with dplyr's `.drop = FALSE`, a factor key
also yields a group for each level that has no rows. Such a group has zero
rows, so `n()` is 0 and `sum()` is 0.

{{< include examples/_group-drop.md >}}

## Distinct rows and joins

`distinct()` keeps the first row of each combination of the given columns.
`join()` takes the other table, the key columns, and the join type: `inner`,
`left`, `right`, `full`, `semi`, `anti`, or `cross`. Joins follow dplyr 1.1,
including its column naming and the rule that NA keys match each other.

{{< include examples/_join.md >}}

Besides equality keys, a join condition can compare columns, as dplyr's
`join_by()` does. `[$left, $op, $right]` with `>=`, `>`, `<=`, or `<` keeps the
pairs that satisfy the comparison, and all conditions must hold. One
`['closest', $left, $op, $right]` condition keeps, for each row of x, only the
y rows with the nearest value: the largest for `>=` and `>`, the smallest for
`<=` and `<`. dplyr's `between()`, `within()`, and `overlaps()` are pairs of
comparisons. In a rolling join, the columns used in comparisons are kept from
both tables:

{{< include examples/_join-by.md >}}

## Immutability

Methods never change the frame they are called on:

{{< include examples/_immutable.md >}}

## Method chains and the pipe operator

Every verb returns a new table, so verbs chain as methods on any PHP version
phibble supports. PHP 8.5's `|>` passes a value to a callable, and arrow
functions let the same pipeline use it. [phplyr](https://github.com/phpstats/phplyr)
provides verbs that return such callables, so a phplyr pipeline needs no arrow
functions.
